When we think of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, we might first think of the chip players making the headlines, from Nvidia to Advanced Micro Devices. We know them for the high-powered graphics processing units (GPUs) that fuel critical AI tasks such as the training and inference of models.

But those chips can't make it to commercialization without another company, and that's Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE: TSM). TSMC is the manufacturer that makes most of today's leading chips, as it holds more than 70% of the global chip foundry market. So while Nvidia, AMD, and others design the chips, TSMC actually brings them from the drawing board to reality.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

All of this has created tremendous growth for TSMC, and the latest earnings report illustrates this. Last week, the company reported record profit for the sixth straight quarter. How does this translate into stock performance? My prediction is that $1,000 invested in TSMC today will be worth this much by 2030...

Image source: Getty Images.
TSMC's market leadership

Before we dive into those numbers, though, let's take a deeper look at TSMC. As mentioned, the company is the global leader in the foundry market, so it produces most of the chips in high demand today. This means that TSMC may benefit from the successes of all of the leading chip players -- not just one or two. And this positions the company very well for significant growth as the AI boom continues.

A look at the recent quarter illustrates the picture. In the third quarter, TSMC reported profit and revenue that surpassed analysts' estimates and forecast fourth-quarter revenue in the range of $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion. At the midpoint, that represents a 58% year-over-year increase.

TSMC's gross margin has declined slightly, and the company forecasts a decrease of 40 basis points to 66% at the midpoint for the fourth quarter. But it's important to keep in mind the reason behind that, and it's linked to growth. TSMC's ramp-up of its 2 nm technology, or next-generation manufacturing process, initially weighs on margins, and the company is also seeing pressure from the costs of its U.S. fabs. But productivity gains should offset this to a certain degree over time.

Importantly, TSMC chief C.C. Wei emphasized the ongoing strength of the AI market. "Recent developments are very positive to AI's long-term demand outlook," he said, noting the increasing adoption of agentic AI and the greater use of open-source AI models.

If you only skimmed the headlines about AMD's MI450 accelerators landing multi-gigawatt deals with Anthropic and Meta, the real surprise sat in the share chart. Holding Advanced Micro Devices from the start of the year would have returned 136.6%, including dividends. If you were deciding on 1 January 2026, before trillion dollar market caps and raised AI forecasts, what would you realistically have needed to believe about AMD's data center push to press "buy"?

The useful thing about a Narrative is that the reasoning is checkable: the assumptions sit beside the argument, and together they imply an estimated Fair Value you can disagree with.

Advanced Micro Devices has already moved. Pinpoint other ways to investigate the theme among 55 AI infrastructure stocks.

The Argument You Would Have Been Weighing Up On AMD

The shares cost US$214 at the start of the period. Anyone looking at Advanced Micro Devices then had to decide whether AI infrastructure could justify paying close to the bullish Fair Value of US$227, or whether that optimism had already gone too far.

The bullish story put Fair Value at US$227. It relied on AI driven data center demand, faster MI350 deployment, and a step up in revenue and margin expansion supported by advanced process nodes and full stack solutions.

The more cautious view landed on a Fair Value of US$185. It treated 20.3% revenue growth and a 17.8% profit margin as ambitious and focused on execution risk, tougher competition, and the strain from heavy AI and adaptive computing investment.

NasdaqGS:AMD Trailing 12-Month Earnings & Revenue History as at Oct 2026
What The AMD Evidence Actually Tested

AMD's Q2 2026 report did the heavy lifting for the bullish case. Revenue moved from US$7,685m in Q2 2025 to US$11,536m, while net income shifted from US$768m to US$2,305m and net margin went from 10.0% to 20.0%. That combination of higher sales and a higher margin supported the more optimistic narrative rather than the cautious one.

The key lesson is simple. When a story depends on both rapid top line expansion and richer profitability, you assess it by tracking revenue and net margin together instead of focusing only on the share chart.

What AMD's 137% Run Already Prices In

Advanced Micro Devices now trades at US$529, after a 136.6% gain from the start of the year. The selected Narrative's Fair Value sits below that level, treating the current quote as demanding rather than cheap.

The thesis leans on AMD's MI350 and future MI400 accelerators turning AI interest into lasting data center earnings. A buyer today effectively assumes that AI hardware ramps smoothly, so QuanD's execution and competitive risks become the pressure test for that belief.

title: 1 Red Flag That AMD Investors Should Be Aware Of Now

1 Red Flag That AMD Investors Should Be Aware Of Now
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 17, 2026 at 9:50 AM MST 4 min read

NVDA
^GSPC

Trading disclosure

Adanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) investors have enjoyed some incredible gains during 2026. Currently, AMD is the ninth-best-performing component of the S&P 500, returning about 160% so far this year. While that figure was closer to 200% before the most recent sell-off, I think this is a wake-up call for most investors.

The reality is that AMD's stock got way too ahead of itself, and its valuation far outpaces its growth expectations. That is a major red flag for investors, and there are a few items investors need to keep an eye on as to when AMD could be a good buy again (hint: It won't be for a while).

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
AMD is gaining ground, but not fast enough

The entire AMD investment thesis circles around AMD catching up to Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) and taking market share. On the surface, it appears that AMD is making headway. It has huge projects like OpenAI's computing cluster, which is starting to be delivered, and is powering Meta Muse from Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META). This has all led to stronger growth for AMD, with its data center division reporting $6.7 billion in revenue and growing by 107%. Overall, this helped the company grow its revenue 50% year over year to $11.5 billion in Q2.

Those are strong results that should be celebrated, but the problem is, it just isn't enough to catch Nvidia. During Q2, Nvidia's data center revenue reached $89 billion, up 117% year over year. Overall revenue rose to $96.2 billion, up 106% year over year. While AMD appears on the surface to be doing better, the reality is that Nvidia's lead is widening.

What makes matters worse is that Nvidia's Q2 results don't include any revenue from its upcoming generation of Vera Rubin architecture chips. This new generation promises major improvements, and they also cost more than previous generations. This will further exaggerate Nvidia's lead over AMD and eliminate the thesis that AMD is catching up.

But don't tell AMD's stock that, because according to it, AMD has won the AI arms race.

AMD's stock has uncoupled from its business

Over the long term, stocks and business growth are highly correlated. Over the short term, any number of factors can influence a stock's price. This is why long-term investing is easier for individual investors, as we can afford to wait for the business results to influence the stock price as long as we've found a company with a great long-term growth thesis.

Key Stats for Intel Stock

Current Price: $89.85

Target Price (Mid): ~$390

Street Target: ~$118

Potential Total Return: ~336%

Annualized IRR: ~42% / year

What Happened?

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM) CEO C.C. Wei signaled on October 15, 2026, that TSMC would support customers who cannot get enough capacity from the EMIB-T packaging of Intel Corporation (INTC). That puts a competitor directly in the path of the foundry business Intel expects to ramp first.

Intel closed at $89.85 on October 16, down 5.79%, in a broad chip selloff that took Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) down 5.95% and Arm Holdings (ARM) down 6.94%. Some outlets also tied Intel's drop to Wei's remarks. On October 14, an explosion at Intel's Kiryat Gat fab in Israel killed two workers, and as of October 16, Intel had not said whether output was affected. Intel reports Q3 results after the close on October 29, per its investor relations materials.

Intel Drawdowns (TIKR)
TSMC Offered Itself as the Backup to Intel's Packaging Push

EMIB-T is Intel's technology for linking AI chips and high-bandwidth memory inside one large package. Wei was answering Morgan Stanley's Charlie Chan, and he called TSMC's CoWoS packaging customers' first choice. TSMC's own lines are tight: in August, Taiwan's Economic Daily News reported some orders spilling from fully booked CoWoS capacity to Intel's Malaysia operations.

EVP and CFO David Zinsner said at an August 26 Deutsche Bank conference that packaging revenue should start ramping in the back half of 2027, ahead of high-volume 14A production in 2028. He expects it to run at around a 40% gross margin and 30% operating margin. Intel has not named a packaging customer, so that timeline rests on management commentary, not disclosed contracts. Intel Foundry lost $10.318 billion at the operating line in fiscal 2025, per TIKR.

Why Packaging Wins Could Delay a 50% Gross Margin

Zinsner still calls a gross margin starting with a 5 the goal, but said Intel is reticent to put a date on it because "some of our businesses actually don't get 50-plus percent gross margins, but they are really high-growth businesses." He put front-end foundry and advanced packaging at around 40% gross margin for now, and many custom ASIC products in the 40s as well.

Intel instead holds each unit to a "Rule of 45," where revenue growth plus operating margin should add up to 45, letting fast growers run thinner margins. Zinsner said not every unit will hit it next year.

Consensus already pencils in the level he won't date. Wall Street models gross margin rising from 36.7% in 2025 to around 54% in 2030, per TIKR, though only seven analysts publish 2030 revenue estimates. Each packaging win adds revenue near a 40% margin, and TSMC competing for the same customers could pressure that pricing. Intel's Q3 guidance midpoint of 42% is up from 39% guided for Q2.

When investors think about AI chipmakers, they may think first of Nvidia or AMD. However, one competitor that most forget about is Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO). Why? It's simple: Broadcom only makes computing units for giant customers, not consumers. However, this is a huge opportunity that shouldn't be ignored, because the growth that Broadcom's management team is guiding for is simply incredible.

If you've got $10,000 sitting around (or any other dollar figure, for that matter), I can think of few better places to invest it, because that $10,000 could be worth $20,000 by the end of 2028.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.
What makes Broadcom different?

AMD and Nvidia make graphics processing units (GPUs), parallel processors that are great at handling a wide range of computationally heavy workloads. GPUs don't have a weakness, but their potential often goes underutilized. Countless GPUs have been stuck running a single type of workload throughout their service life, which leaves some of their incredible capabilities wasted. AI hyperscalers would be better off using a purpose-built computing chip in these applications, which is where Broadcom steps in.

Broadcom partners with its hyperscaler clients to design custom AI computing units powered by proprietary chips that only have the capacities that the client's workloads require. While these units aren't as flexible as GPUs, they provide far better cost performance than a GPU on properly configured workloads. This helps AI hyperscalers maximize their computing potential at lower cost, which is particularly appealing as funds become harder to come by.

Broadcom has several big-name clients, including Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL), Meta Platforms, Anthropic, and OpenAI. While all of its clients are ramping up their AI infrastructure spending, none have had a more successful product than Alphabet. Alphabet and Broadcom collaborated to design the Tensor Processing Unit (TPU). This unit has been around for a while, and has gone through several generations. Google Cloud clients can rent access to TPUs on that computing platform. But TPUs are so impressive that Alphabet has begun to expand beyond leasing their compute power in its data centers, and is now starting to sell them directly to external customers like Meta as well.
